review.reason: Read primary results, discussion and methods; distinguish measured aerodynamics from proposed evolutionary tradeoffs.

item.title: Nightjars trade off cruising speed efficiency for hovering capabilities and link upstroke thrust production with restricted wing folding
item.headline: A nightjar’s wings reveal the compromises of flight
item.authors: L. Christoffer Johansson, Gabriel Norevik, Sonja Friman and Anders Hedenström
item.summary: Wind-tunnel measurements of three European nightjars suggest compromises between slow flight and cruising. Lift production became less efficient at higher speeds, even as estimated energy per distance decreased.

evidence.question: How do nightjar wings meet competing flight demands?
evidence.method: Measured air wakes and filmed wing movements at 2.6–11 m/s; models accounted for repeated observations of individuals.
evidence.limitations: Three selected birds; forces and power were inferred from wakes, without measuring metabolic expenditure.

explainer.finding: Paired wingtip vortices accompanied reduced lift efficiency at cruising speeds. The outer wings also generated thrust during the upstroke.
explainer.method: Particle tracking measured airflow; high-speed cameras reconstructed wing motion. These measurements supported force and power estimates.
explainer.meaning: Catching insects slowly and migrating quickly place different demands on the same wings. Efficient lift production and economical travel are different measures of success.
explainer.limits: Wing shape was not experimentally changed. Its proposed benefits for hovering remain an interpretation; low-speed wing–wake interactions may affect power estimates.
